targets.authors: Carney, D. R., Cuddy, A. J., & Yap, A. J.
targets.title: Power posing brief nonverbal displays aﬀect neuroendocrine levels and risk tolerance.
targets.evidence_quote:
First, we intended to replicate Carney
et al.’s (2010) main eﬀects and to test the possibility that the relationship between
embodied power and risk-taking is statistically mediated by increases in testosterone.
targets.outcome_quote:
In contrast to Carney et al. (2010), we ﬁnd no support for the hypothesis that power
posing aﬀects subjective feelings of power or risk-taking. Nor do we ﬁnd any evidence
that power posing changes testosterone, cortisol, or the additionally proposed interac-
tion between testosterone and cortisol.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors explicitly conclude that their new-sample replication does not support the original power-pose effects. The overall verdict is failed; discussion of possible moderators does not declare the attempt uninformative.

targets.authors: Fast, N. J., Sivanathan, N., Mayer, N. D., & Galinsky, A. D.
targets.title: Power and overconﬁdent decision-making.
targets.evidence_quote:
Building from these ﬁndings, Fast and colleagues (2012)
reported ﬁve experiments that used multiple instantiations of power – including manip-
ulations via episodic recall tasks, role assignment, and extant work related power –
where they found high power to be associated with overconﬁdent decision-making.
Based on these ﬁndings, we propose that exaggerated expressions of conﬁdence will
emerge as a function of the degree to which high-power poses facilitate a high-power
mind-set.
targets.outcome_quote:
High-power (M = 0.14, SD = 0.53) posers did not have higher post-manipulation levels of
overconﬁdence than low-power posers (M = −0.01, SD = 0.51), F(1,104) = 0.26, p = 0.61,
d = 0.099, r = 0.05.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The extension directly tests the published power-to-overconfidence relationship using embodied power. The introduction states the original positive finding and derives this study’s prediction from it; the new-sample comparison fails to show it. This is a conceptual retest, even though called an extension.

targets.authors: Mehta, P. H., Welker, K. M., Zilioli, S., & Carré, J. M.
targets.title: Testosterone and cortisol jointly modulate risk-taking.
targets.evidence_quote:
Because Carney et al.
(2010) found high-power poses to both increase testosterone and decrease cortisol, the
interaction between these eﬀects may predict risk-taking, as has been previously shown
(Mehta et al., 2015). Furthermore, although Ranehill et al. (2015) failed to replicate
Carney et al.’s (2010) eﬀects of power posing on hormonal changes, other manipulations
related to power, such as winning a competition, have been shown to jointly impact
testosterone and cortisol (e.g. see Hamilton, Carré, Mehta, Olmstead, & Whitaker, 2015).
Thus, in the present research, we measured both testosterone and cortisol at two time
points, as per Carney et al.’s (2010) original design and tested for both main and
interactive eﬀects.
targets.outcome_quote:
The interaction
between post-manipulation testosterone and cortisol was also unrelated to gambling
decisions, z = 0.02, p = 0.90, φ = 0.037.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The paper explicitly invokes the previously shown testosterone-by-cortisol prediction of risk-taking, then measures both hormones to test their interactive effects in its own sample. The corresponding interaction is unrelated to gambling decisions, contrary to that published prediction.

reasoning: The completed experiment collected new Dutch-participant data. It directly replicates Carney et al. (2010) and conceptually retests the explicitly specified power-overconfidence finding of Fast et al. (2012) and hormone-interaction/risk-taking finding of Mehta et al. (2015). Ranehill et al. (2015) is an earlier replication discussed as context; the paper deliberately follows Carney’s design. The 2015 Carney paper is commentary rather than the original finding. Other overconfidence/risk-taking references motivate the new mediated pathway, involving distinct skill-dependent decisions, and are not independently specified retests. Johnson et al. (2006) is background for a new fluctuation hypothesis: its reported association disappears controlling gender, whereas this paper proposes a within-design hormone-change pathway. No original-data reproduction is reported.
